'''Arland Richard Bruce III''' (born November 23, 1977) is an American former professional [[gridiron football|football]] [[wide receiver]] who played in the [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL) and [[National Football League]] (NFL). He is a two-time [[Grey Cup]] champion, having won in [[92nd Grey Cup|2004]] with the [[Toronto Argonauts]] and in [[99th Grey Cup|2011]] with the [[BC Lions]]. He played 12 seasons in the CFL with the [[Winnipeg Blue Bombers]], Toronto Argonauts, [[Hamilton Tiger-Cats]], [[BC Lions]], and [[Montreal Alouettes]]. During the [[2011 BC Lions season|2011 season]], he became the 14th CFL receiver to record over 10,000 yards receiving in a career. Bruce also played in the NFL for the [[San Francisco 49ers]].

==Early life==
Bruce attended [[Olathe North High School]] in [[Olathe, Kansas]], and was a [[Letterman (sports)|letterman]] in [[High school football|football]]. As a senior, he was a BlueChip Illustrated Top-100 pick, the Kansas State Player of the Year, and finished the year with 1,696 rushing yards.  Bruce finished his high school career with more than 3,000 rushing yards and 50 touchdowns.

==College career==
Bruce then attended [[Hutchinson Community College]] in [[Hutchinson, Kansas]]. As a freshman, he was named a First-team [[All-America]]n selection and rushed for over 1,000 yards. During his sophomore season, he ran for 997 yards and 10 touchdowns and was named a Second-team All-American selection.

Bruce transferred to play for the [[Minnesota Golden Gophers football|University of Minnesota]].  As a senior, he helped lead his team to an 8–3 record and a [[Sun Bowl]] berth.

==Professional career==
===Kansas City Chiefs===
On April 19, 2000, Bruce was signed by the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] of the NFL. He was waived on August 27 and later signed to the team's [[practice squad]] on September 19, 2000.<ref name="transactions">{{cite web | url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/transactions/b/bruc00130.html | title=Arland Bruce NFL Transactions | publisher=profootballarchives.com | accessdate=15 October 2024}}</ref>

===Winnipeg Blue Bombers===
On May 1, 2001, Bruce joined the CFL's [[Winnipeg Blue Bombers]] where he got his first opportunity as a professional to receive significant playing time, playing in all 18 regular season games.  In his rookie season, Bruce had 818 receiving yards with 7 touchdowns.  His team went on to play in the [[Grey Cup]] championship, only to lose to the [[Calgary Stampeders]].

In 2002, Bruce surpassed the 1000 yard receiving mark by amassing 1062 receiving yards with 12 touchdowns in 17 games.

===San Francisco 49ers===
In 2003, Bruce returned to the U.S. to try his luck once more with the NFL.  On March 3 of that year, he signed with the [[San Francisco 49ers]] where he spent much of his playing time on [[special teams]]. He was waived on August 30, 2004.<ref name="transactions"/>

===Toronto Argonauts===
In 2004, after being released by the 49ers following their training camp, Bruce returned to the CFL with the [[Toronto Argonauts]], signing with them on September 3, more than halfway through the CFL season and just shortly before their [[Labour Day Classic]] game against the [[Hamilton Tiger-Cats]] in which he played.  For the remaining seven games in the regular season, Bruce had 247 receiving yards with just one touchdown.  In addition to playing receiver, Bruce also served as one of two [[kick returner]]s on the team alongside incumbent [[Bashir Levingston]].  In that role, Bruce returned two kick returns for touchdowns that season.  In the East Division final, Bruce led all receivers with 12 receptions for 101 yards, and returned a kickoff 97 yards for a touchdown in the first quarter, helping the Argonauts advance to the [[Grey Cup]] championship that year.  In the big game, the kick returning threat of both Bruce & Levingston induced the opposing [[BC Lions]] to punt the ball out of bounds for much of the game to neutralize the threat.  In addition, Bruce was once again a go to receiver amassing 79 yards on 5 receptions.  Bruce and the Argos went on to win the Grey Cup.

[[File:Arland Bruce in 2005.JPG|Bruce in 2005 at Rogers Centre in Toronto, Ontario.|thumb|right]]
In 2005, Bruce established himself as the Argonauts top receiver with 1205 receiving yards and 11 touchdowns.  In that same year, Bruce was named an East division [[all-star]] marking the first time in his CFL career he had ever been named to an all-star team.

In 2008, after acquiring a touchdown against the [[Hamilton Tiger-Cats]], Bruce was fined an undisclosed amount by the CFL for donning a [[Spider-Man]] mask during his touchdown celebration.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sportsnet.ca/football/cfl/bruce-spiderman-mask-fine/ |title=Costly costume: CFL fines Argos' WR |access-date=2020-09-22 |publisher=SPORTSNET.CA |date=2009-09-14 }}</ref>

In 2009, he received two objectionable conduct penalties and an undisclosed fine from the CFL for a touchdown celebration against the Tiger-Cats on July 1, in which he removed his helmet, jersey, and [[Shoulder pads (sport)|shoulder pads]], and laid down in the end zone in what he said was a tribute to the recently deceased [[Celebrity|pop star]], [[Michael Jackson]].<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.nydailynews.com/sports/2009/07/02/2009-07-02_cfl_player_penalized_for_jackson_tribute_.html|title=CFL player Arland Bruce penalized for Michael Jackson tribute|last=Wiener|first=Jon|date=2009-07-02|work=New York Daily News|access-date=2009-07-02}}</ref> The Argonauts publicly supported the fine and disciplined Bruce additionally and he apologized to teammates at a team meeting the following day. [[Head coach]] [[Bart Andrus]] took some responsibility on himself, however, noting that, "I made the mistake of telling him in camp that once he got to the end zone I didn't care what he did but he's straight with it now and I think next time around he will celebrate in an appropriate manner."<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.sportsnet.ca/football/cfl/2009/07/02/cfl_argos_bruce_review/|title=Bruce fined for Jackson tribute|last=Lefko|first=Perry|date=2009-07-02|publisher=Sportsnet.ca|access-date=2009-07-02}}</ref>

===Hamilton Tiger-Cats===
On July 29, 2009, Bruce was traded to the Hamilton Tiger-Cats in exchange for the rights to [[Corey Mace]], a third round pick in the [[2010 CFL draft]], and a conditional third round pick in the [[2011 CFL draft]] a week after a dispute with coach Andrus became public and Bruce was left home for the Week 4 game in Winnipeg.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.tsn.ca/cfl/story/?id=286077|title=Argonauts trade receiver Bruce to Tiger-Cats|date=2009-07-29|publisher=TSN|access-date=2009-07-29}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=http://network.nationalpost.com/np/blogs/postedsports/archive/2009/07/29/arland-bruce-iii-shipped-to-hamilton-for-draft-pick-prospect.aspx |title=Arland Bruce III shipped to Hamilton for picks, prospect |last=Fitz-Gerald |first=Sean |date=2009-07-29 |newspaper=National Post |access-date=2009-07-29 }}{{dead link|date=October 2025|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref>

In July 2011, Bruce declared his intention to change his name to "Runako Reth".<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.torontosun.com/2011/07/20/bruce-leads-ticats-in-the-bizarre |title=CFL: Bruce leads Ticats in the bizarre |access-date=2011-07-22 |publisher=Toronto Sun |date=2011-07-20}}</ref>

===BC Lions===
On August 3, 2011, Bruce was traded to the [[BC Lions]] in exchange for a third-round draft pick in the [[2012 CFL draft]] and an additional conditional draft pick in the 2013 CFL Draft.<ref>https://www.cfl.ca/article/ticats-trade-receiver-bruce-to-lions {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120923152620/http://www.cfl.ca/article/ticats-trade-receiver-bruce-to-lions |date=2012-09-23 }} Ticats trade receiver Bruce to Lions</ref> Bruce had a productive season with the [[BC Lions|Lions]], recording 49 catches for 755 yards and eight touchdowns in 12 games. In the [[99th Grey Cup]] game against the [[Winnipeg Blue Bombers]], he had 73 yards receiving and a touchdown and won his second championship. During the following off-season, he signed a contract extension with the Lions.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://cfl.ca/article/arland-bruce-extends-with-grey-cup-champs_91869|title=Bruce resigns with the BC Lions|access-date=2012-01-26|publisher=CFL.ca|date=2012-01-26|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120128215806/http://www.cfl.ca/article/arland-bruce-extends-with-grey-cup-champs_91869|archive-date=2012-01-28|url-status=dead}}</ref> On January 18, 2013, Bruce was released by the BC Lions.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cfl.ca/article/lions-release-former-all-stars-bruce-and-parker|title=Bruce released by the BC Lions|access-date=2013-01-19|publisher=CFL.ca|date=2013-01-18|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130121133745/http://www.cfl.ca/article/lions-release-former-all-stars-bruce-and-parker|archive-date=2013-01-21|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===Montreal Alouettes===
On January 21, 2013, Bruce signed with the [[Montreal Alouettes]] of the [[Canadian Football League]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.cfl.ca/article/making-a-splash-als-sign-bruce-parker-and-porter|title=Porter signs with the Alouettes|last=Milton|first=Steve|date=2013-01-21|publisher=CFL.ca|access-date=2012-01-21|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130124083302/http://www.cfl.ca/article/making-a-splash-als-sign-bruce-parker-and-porter|archive-date=2013-01-24|url-status=dead}}</ref> Arland Bruce had a respectable 2013 season with the Alouettes. He contributed 64 pass receptions, his most since 2010, for 851 yards with 5 touchdowns. In February 2014, Bruce was fined an undisclosed amount by the CFL following his Instagram post in which he told openly gay NFL prospect [[Michael Sam]] to, "get on his knees and submit to God fully".<ref>[http://www.cbc.ca/sports/football/cfl/arland-bruce-bryant-turner-jr-fined-for-anti-gay-remarks-1.2532734 Arland Bruce, Bryant Turner Jr. fined for anti-gay remarks]</ref> Bruce was released by the Alouettes in late February. Bruce's high salary along with the belief that new head coach [[Tom Higgins (Canadian football)|Tom Higgins]] would start two Canadian wide receivers were cited as the reasons for his dismissal.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.tsn.ca/cfl/story/?id=444752|title=Alouettes cut ties with veteran receiver Bruce III|date=2014-02-26|publisher=TSN.ca|access-date=2014-02-26}}</ref>

'''Arthur Barry Still''' (born December 5, 1955) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive end]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Kentucky Wildcats football|Kentucky Wildcats]], earning unanimous [[1977 College Football All-America Team|All-American]] honors in 1977. He played professionally for the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] (1978–1987) and the [[Buffalo Bills]] (1988–1989).

==College career==
Still played at Kentucky under head coach [[Fran Curci]] and led the defense on the [[1977 Kentucky Wildcats football team]] that finished 10-1 and ranked #6 in the final AP poll. On January 9, 2015, the National Football Foundation announced that Still would be inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame.

==Professional career==
Still was the second overall player taken in the [[1978 NFL draft]] and became an immediate [[Starting lineup|starter]] for the Chiefs, making the NFL All-[[Rookie]] Team in 1978.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1978 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1978/draft.htm |access-date=2023-12-30 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> In 1979 Still began to get more notice and was voted Second-team All-[[American Football Conference|AFC]] by [[United Press International|UPI]]. In 1980, Still recorded an unofficial 14.5 [[Quarterback sack|sacks]], sacks were not officially counted until 1982, and was voted [[1980 All-Pro Team|All-Pro]] and All-AFC as well as being named to the [[Pro Bowl]]. The following year, 1981, he was voted to his second Pro Bowl. In 1982, he made it three Pro Bowls in a row and was voted second-team All-AFC. In 1983 Still went on an all-[[Vegetarianism|vegetarian diet]] and played at 235 pounds, and it seemingly broke his string of post-season honors in the NFL. In 1984, he was back to 265 pounds and was Second-team [[1984 All-Pro Team|All-Pro]] and a Pro Bowler. That season he recorded 14.5 sacks. In 1985, he played solidly but failed to make any All-Pro or All-AFC teams. However, in 1986 he recorded 10.5 sacks and was named First-team All-AFC as the Chiefs made the playoffs.

Still was a 4-time [[Pro Bowl]] selection, following the 1980-1982 and 1984 seasons, named the [[Kansas City Chiefs]]'s Most Valuable Player twice (1980 and 1984). Still is third on the Chiefs all-time sack list with 48.5 and has also made 922 [[tackle (football move)|tackles]] and 11 [[fumble]] recoveries. He led the team in sacks on 6 occasions, twice registering 14.5 in a season and topped the team's tackle chart 3 times. He was traded to the Buffalo Bills in 1988 and played there for 2 seasons.

==Personal life==
Art Still's younger sister, [[Valerie Still]], is the all-time leading scorer and rebounder in [[University of Kentucky]] basketball history among men and women. His cousin is former [[Houston Texans]] [[defensive tackle]] [[Devon Still]]. He also has 3 sons and a daughter who are Kansas City Missouri fire fighters.<ref name="postgazette">{{cite news | url = http://www.post-gazette.com/pg/11258/1174804-143-0.stm | title = Lineman Still enjoys being disruptive force on defense | newspaper = [[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]] | first = Ron | last = Musselman | date = 2011-09-15}}</ref>

'''Arnold Harrison II''' (born September 20, 1982) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was signed by the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] as an [[undrafted free agent]] in 2005. He played [[college football]] for the [[Georgia Bulldogs football|Georgia Bulldogs]].

Harrison also played for the [[Cleveland Browns]] and [[Florida Tuskers]].

==College career==
Harrison played [[college football]] at the [[University of Georgia]] where he majored in economics.

==Professional career==

===Pittsburgh Steelers===
Harrison was signed by the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] as an [[undrafted free agent]] in 2005, but did not make any appearances for the team in his rookie season.

In 2006, he played in seven games and finished the season with ten tackles. He appeared in 13 games in 2007 and recorded 13 tackles.

After spending the entire 2008 season on [[injured reserve]] with a torn [[Anterior cruciate ligament|ACL]], Harrison was non-tendered as a [[restricted free agent]] in the 2009 offseason. However, the Steelers re-signed him to a one-year contract on March 16.<ref>{{Cite web |date=March 16, 2009 |title=Steelers sign Frazier and Harrison |url=https://www.steelers.com/news/steelers-sign-frazier-and-harrison-959618 |website=www.steelers.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

Harrison appeared in eight games and recorded seven tackles for the Steelers in 2009 before being waived on November 17 to make room for [[linebacker]] [[Donovan Woods (American football)|Donovan Woods]].

===Cleveland Browns===
Harrison was claimed off waivers by the [[Cleveland Browns]] on November 18. He appeared in four games and recorded five tackles for the Browns before being waived on December 29 when the team re-signed [[offensive tackle]] [[Scott Kooistra]].

'''Arlen Quincy Harris Sr.''' (born April 22, 1980) is a former [[National Football League|NFL]] running back who played for the [[St. Louis Rams]], [[Detroit Lions]], and the [[Atlanta Falcons]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[University of Virginia]] and [[Hofstra University]].  He won a [[Pennsylvania Interscholastic Athletic Association|PIAA]] State Championship at [[Downingtown High School]] as a player in 1997. He won a MSHSAA State Championship at Lutheran St. Charles in 2021 as the head varsity coach, named Coach of the Year along with his oldest son AJ receiving Offensive POY and his youngest son Ayden Defensive POY.

==Biography==
Arlen was born in Chester, Pennsylvania,<ref>{{cite web |last1=Starkey |first1=Joe |title=Play of the Game: Harris breaks loose |url=https://archive.triblive.com/news/play-of-the-game-harris-breaks-loose-2/ |website=www.archive.triblive.com |access-date=20 May 2020}}</ref>  and was considered one of the top 3 running backs coming out of [[Downingtown High School]] where he won a PIAA State Championship and broke Tony Dorsett's rushing record. He was a Parade All-American. He also played in the Big 33 All-Star game vs the top players in Ohio and won [[most valuable player|MVP]].
In college, Harris did not play his junior year, due to an injury to his knee, or his senior year because he transferred and lost that year's eligibility. So, Harris did not play football for two years until he made his return to football in the Paradise Bowl [[all-star game]] in [[Las Vegas Valley|Las Vegas]] and was named MVP.<ref>McPherson, Chris. [http://www.dailylocal.com/article/20031030/SPORTS03/310309977/harris-enjoying-success-in-st-louis#full_story "Harris enjoying success in St. Louis"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160311001957/http://www.dailylocal.com/article/20031030/SPORTS03/310309977/harris-enjoying-success-in-st-louis#full_story |date=2016-03-11 }}. ''[[Daily Local News]]'', October 30, 2003. Retrieved on May 27, 2013.</ref>

Harris was undrafted in the [[2003 NFL draft]], and signed with the NFL's [[St. Louis Rams]]. He played three seasons with the Rams, starting three games and scoring three touchdowns versus the Steelers' #1 defense.<ref>[[Pete Palmer|Palmer, Pete]]; Pullis, Ken; [[Sean Lahman|Lahman, Sean]]; Silverman, Matthew; [[Gary Gillette|Gillette, Gary]] (Eds.). ''The ESPN Pro Football Encyclopedia: First Edition'', p. 291. [[ESPN Books]], 2006. {{ISBN|978-1-4027-4216-3}}.</ref> He moved to the [[Detroit Lions]] in 2006, also starting three games there.<ref>''CBS Sports''. [http://www.cbssports.com/nfl/players/playerpage/396971 "Arlen Harris, NFL"]. Retrieved on May 27, 2013.</ref> He ended his career with the Atlanta Falcons with a knee injury in the last [[pre-season]] game against the [[Baltimore Ravens]].

Harris and his wife, Heather, have three children, Caeli, Arlen Jr., and Ayden.

In 2017, Harris was inducted into the Chester County Sports Hall of Fame.<ref>{{cite web |title=Arlen Harris |url=http://www.chestercountysportshalloffame.com/inductees/2017/arlen_harris.html |website=www.chestercountysportshalloffame.com |access-date=20 May 2020}}</ref>

In 2018, Harris was inducted into the Downingtown High School Hall of Fame.

'''Arron Eugene Sears''' (born October 25, 1984) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Guard (American football)|guard]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Tennessee Volunteers football|Tennessee Volunteers]] and was selected by the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] in the second round of the [[2007 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2007 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2007/draft.htm |access-date=May 11, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

==Early life==
Sears attended [https://www.rcs.k12.al.us/site/Default.aspx?PageID=15 Russellville High School] in [[Russellville, Alabama]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=May 2, 2007 |title=Sears brothers set to make NFL debut |url=https://franklincountytimes.com/2007/05/02/sears-brothers-set-to-make-nfl-debut/ |access-date=March 15, 2024 |website=Franklin County Times}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Aaron Sears, 2003 Offensive Tackle, Tennessee |url=https://rivals.com/content/athletes/aaron-sears-72952?view=pv |access-date=March 15, 2024 |website=Rivals.com |language=en-US}}</ref> He was considered a top high school prospect and was invited to participate in the [[U.S. Army All-American Bowl]]. Sears was also named the 5A lineman of the year in [[Alabama]] by High School Sports Magazine.

==College career==
Sears was a starter at the [[University of Tennessee]] after taking over at the end of his freshman year against [[Mississippi State Bulldogs|Mississippi State]].  He started at several positions on the [[offensive line]] but mostly at tackle. During his career, Sears received All-America and All-SEC honors. He was a team captain on the [[2006 Tennessee Volunteers football team]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Arron Sears - Football |url=https://utsports.com/sports/football/roster/arron-sears/12204 |access-date=March 15, 2024 |website=University of Tennessee Athletics |language=en}}</ref> He has an older brother (Kevin Sears) who played [[linebacker]] for [[Auburn University]], and they faced each other twice in the 2004 season.

==Professional career==
Sears was named the Buccaneers' starter at left guard from Week 1 and did not disappoint, garnering a selection to the [[PFWA NFL All-Rookie Team|2007 NFL All-Rookie Team]] for his efforts.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2007 NFL All-Rookie Team |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/awards/nfl-all-rookie-2007.htm |access-date=March 15, 2024 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

Arron Sears started all 31 of his career games in his two seasons in the NFL.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Arron Sears Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/S/SearAr20.htm |access-date=March 15, 2024 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

On June 2, 2009, it was reported that Sears had a [[neurological]] condition sustained from a [[concussion]]. The extent of the injury was unknown, but early reports said it was possibly severe enough to be career-threatening.<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 17, 2009 |title=Sears Non-Starter |url=https://www.bucsnation.com/2009/6/17/912454/sears-non-starter |access-date=March 15, 2024 |website=Bucs Nation |language=en}}</ref> He would ultimately leave the team and not return.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Katzowitz |first=Josh  |date=June 28, 2012 |title=Former Bucs G Arron Sears, 27, suffering from neurological problems |url=https://www.cbssports.com/nfl/news/former-bucs-g-arron-sears-27-suffering-from-neurological-problems/ |access-date=March 15, 2024 |website=CBSSports.com |language=en}}</ref>

Sears was waived by the Buccaneers on April 26, 2010.<ref>{{Cite web |date=April 26, 2010 |title=Bucs Release Six, Including Hovan, Sears |url=https://www.buccaneers.com/news/bucs-release-six-including-hovan-sears-2262983 |access-date=March 15, 2024 |website=Buccaneers.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Personal life==
By age 27, Sears felt a "total loss of function" and was said to have swings of anger that could be a risk to others.<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 28, 2012 |title=At age 27, ex-Buc Arron Sears has "almost total loss of function" |url=https://www.nbcsports.com/nfl/profootballtalk/rumor-mill/news/at-age-27-ex-buc-arron-sears-has-almost-total-loss-of-function |access-date=March 15, 2024 |website=NBC Sports |language=en-US}}</ref> He was held for a mental health evaluation after being found wandering on the highway in 2010.<ref>{{Cite web |date=November 16, 2010 |title=NFL Roundup: Former Bucs Star Rookie Sears Arrested |url=https://www.theledger.com/story/news/2010/11/17/nfl-roundup-former-bucs-star-rookie-sears-arrested/26401041007/ |access-date=March 15, 2024 |website=The Ledger |language=en-US}}</ref> Sears sued the NFL and the Buccaneers in 2012 because of the head trauma he experienced in his career leaving him unable to care for himself.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hanstock |first=Bill |date=June 28, 2012 |title=Arron Sears Is 'Unable To Care for Himself', Files Concussion Lawsuit |url=https://www.sbnation.com/nfl/2012/6/28/3124166/arron-sears-tampa-bay-buccaneers-concussion |access-date=March 15, 2024 |website=SBNation.com |language=en}}</ref>

'''Armanti Fredrico Edwards Sr.''' (born March 8, 1988) is an American former professional [[gridiron football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] in the [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL) and [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] as a [[quarterback]] for the [[Appalachian State Mountaineers football|Appalachian State Mountaineers]] from 2006 to 2009, and was named a 2024 inductee of [[College Football Hall of Fame]].<ref name="2024 COLLEGE FOOTBALL HALL OF FAME CLASS">{{Cite news |last=National Football Foundation (NFF) & College Hall of Fame |date=January 8, 2024 |title=NFF Announces Star-Studded 2024 College Football Hall of Fame Class |publisher=NFF |url=https://footballfoundation.org/news/2024/1/8/nff-announces-star-studded-2024-college-football-hall-of-fame-class.aspx |access-date=January 21, 2024}}</ref> Edwards led Appalachian State to one of the biggest upsets in college football history, [[2007 Appalachian State vs. Michigan football game|a 34–32 victory over then fifth-ranked Michigan]] in 2007. He was selected by the [[Carolina Panthers]] in the third round of the [[2010 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Andrew Mason |date=April 23, 2010 |title=After QB, Panthers target targets |publisher=Panthers.com |url=http://www.panthers.com/news/article-1/After-QB-Panthers-target-targets/ff6fd4fd-4ee9-4ea2-be7d-ec0b077b551e |url-status=dead |access-date=April 24, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100428205659/http://www.panthers.com/news/article-1/After-QB-Panthers-target-targets/ff6fd4fd-4ee9-4ea2-be7d-ec0b077b551e |archive-date=April 28, 2010}}</ref> In 2017, Edwards won the [[105th Grey Cup|Grey Cup]] with the [[2017 Toronto Argonauts season|Toronto Argonauts]]. He last played for the CFL's [[Edmonton Elks]].

In addition to leading Appalachian State to consecutive [[NCAA Division I Football Championship]]s (FCS) in [[2006 Appalachian State Mountaineers football team|2006]] and [[2007 Appalachian State Mountaineers football team|2007]], Edwards became the first quarterback in [[Southern Conference]] history to lead his team to four straight conference [[List of Southern Conference football champions|championships]].<ref name="5Titles">{{Cite news |last=Appalachian Sports Information |date=November 14, 2009 |title=Mountaineers Clinch Fifth-Straight SoCon Title |publisher=GoASU |url=http://www.goasu.com/ViewArticle.dbml?SPSID=104460&SPID=12811&DB_OEM_ID=21500&ATCLID=204833726 |access-date=November 19, 2009}}</ref> He became the first quarterback in [[National Collegiate Athletic Association|NCAA]] [[Division I (NCAA)|Division I]] history to throw for 9,000 and rush for 4,000 yards in a career, accomplishing the feat against [[Furman Paladins football|Furman]] on October 31, 2009.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Appalachian Sports Information |date=October 31, 2009 |title=Mountaineers Rout Furman, 52–27 |publisher=GoASU |url=http://www.goasu.com/ViewArticle.dbml?SPSID=104460&SPID=12811&DB_OEM_ID=21500&ATCLID=204824766 |access-date=November 19, 2009}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Jason Gilmer |date=November 19, 2009 |title=Did He Just Do That? |publisher=High Country Press |url=http://www.highcountrypress.com/weekly/2009/11-19-09/did-he-just-do-that.htm |url-status=dead |access-date=November 19, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110711165601/http://www.highcountrypress.com/weekly/2009/11-19-09/did-he-just-do-that.htm |archive-date=July 11, 2011}}</ref> Later in the [[2009 NCAA Division I FCS football season|season]], he would become the first quarterback to pass for over 10,000 yards and rush for an additional 4,000 yards in a career.<ref>{{Cite news |date=December 18, 2009 |title=Edwards takes it: ASU quarterback wins the Walter Payton Award for the second time |publisher=Winston-Salem Journal |url=http://www2.journalnow.com/content/2009/dec/18/edwards-takes-it/ |url-status=dead |access-date=April 4, 2010 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120826023228/http://www2.journalnow.com/content/2009/dec/18/edwards-takes-it/ |archive-date=August 26, 2012}}</ref> He is also the first back-to-back and two-time [[Walter Payton Award]] winner, given to the [[Division I (NCAA)#Football Championship Subdivision|Football Championship Subdivision]]'s most outstanding offensive player, receiving the award in 2008 and 2009.<ref name="AEPayton2">{{Cite news |title=Armanti Edwards wins 2009 Walter Payton Award |publisher=The Sports Network |url=http://www.sportsnetwork.com/merge/tsnform.aspx?c=sportsnetwork&page=cfoot2/misc/2009payton_edwards_900.htm |url-status=dead |access-date=December 17, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110404060532/http://www.sportsnetwork.com/merge/tsnform.aspx?c=sportsnetwork&page=cfoot2%2Fmisc%2F2009payton_edwards_900.htm |archive-date=April 4, 2011}}</ref><ref name="AEPayton3">{{Cite news |title=Edwards wins second Payton Award |publisher=ESPN |agency=Associated Press |url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/news/story?id=4753204 |access-date=December 17, 2009}}</ref>

{{TOClimit|limit=4}}

==Early life==
Armanti is the son of Deborah Anderson and Freddie Edwards. At birth, Edwards weighed 4 pounds 11 ounces and was delivered 10 days late.<ref name="Evans">{{Cite news |last=Thayer Evans |date=August 29, 2008 |title=A Father's Prediction Becomes a Son's Tribute |work=New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/08/30/sports/ncaafootball/30edwards.html?ref=sports |access-date=December 4, 2008}}</ref> In September 2006, his father, Freddie, was convicted of a 2005 murder and sentenced to 30 years in prison. The conviction however was overturned because jurors were not given the option of finding Edwards guilty of involuntary manslaughter. During a retrial that concluded in June 2011 he was again convicted of murder and again sentenced to 30 years.<ref name="Evans" />

==High school career==
At [[Greenwood High School (South Carolina)|Greenwood High]], under coach Shell Dula, he was named to the Greenwood Touchdown Club/Index-Journal All-Lakelands Team. Edwards originally played wide receiver, but in his senior year, he moved under center. The transition occurred late in the recruiting process, and he drew some interest from [[New Mexico State Aggies football|New Mexico State]], [[Memphis Tigers football|Memphis]], [[South Carolina Gamecocks football|South Carolina]], and [[Vanderbilt Commodores football|Vanderbilt]]. After only receiving an offer from [[New Mexico State Aggies football|New Mexico State]], he decided to honor his commitment to Appalachian State, in part because they would let him stay a quarterback. Armanti Edwards graduated with a 3.3 [[Grading in education#United States|GPA]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Anthony Stalter |date=August 20, 2008 |title=Is Appalachian State's Armanti Edwards a true Heisman candidate? |url=http://www.scoresreport.com/2008/08/20/is-appalachian-state%E2%80%99s-armanti-edwards-a-true-heisman-candidate/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081206153649/http://www.scoresreport.com/2008/08/20/is-appalachian-state%E2%80%99s-armanti-edwards-a-true-heisman-candidate/ |archive-date=December 6, 2008 |access-date=November 29, 2008 |publisher=The Scores Report}}</ref>

==College career==

===2006 season===
Armanti Edwards led the Mountaineers to the FCS (formerly Division I-AA) [[NCAA Division I Football Championship|National Championship]] in [[2006 Appalachian State Mountaineers football team|2006]] as a [[true freshman]], beating the [[UMass Minutemen football|Minutemen]] of [[University of Massachusetts Amherst|UMass]] 28–17. He finished the 2006 season with 2,251 yards and 15 touchdowns passing, and 1,153 yards and 15 touchdowns rushing. Edwards joined a select list as the fifth [[Division I (NCAA)|Division I]] player (Missouri's [[Brad Smith (American football, born 1983)|Brad Smith]] and Texas's [[Vince Young]] are among the others), and second freshman, to accomplish the feat of 2000 passing yards and 1000 rushing yards in one season.<ref name="Schlabach">{{Cite web |last=Mark Schlabach |date=September 20, 2007 |title=Undersized and overlooked, Edwards shines at Big House |url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/notebook?page=gamedayFinal071 |access-date=December 4, 2008 |publisher=ESPN}}</ref> Edwards was named the [[Southern Conference]] Freshman of the Year at the end of the season.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Appalachian Sports Information |date=November 22, 2006 |title=Mountaineers Clean Up as SoCon Awards, All-Conference Teams are Announced |publisher=GoASU |url=http://www.goasu.com/ViewArticle.dbml?SPSID=104458&SPID=12811&DB_OEM_ID=21500&ATCLID=1543817 |access-date=December 4, 2008}}</ref>

===2007 season===
Edwards started the [[2007 Appalachian State Mountaineers football team|2007 season]] by guiding Appalachian State to a [[2007 Appalachian State vs. Michigan football game|34–32 upset victory]] over [[2007 NCAA Division I FBS football rankings|fifth-ranked]] [[Michigan Wolverines football|Michigan]] of the Football Bowl Subdivision on September 1, in a game that was named the "Biggest Upset of 2007" by ''[[Sports Illustrated]]''.<ref name="si121307">{{Cite news |date=December 13, 2007 |title=Biggest Upsets of 2007: No. 1 Appalachian State 34, No. 5 Michigan 32 |publisher=Sports Illustrated |url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/multimedia/photo_gallery/0712/cfb.upsets/content.10.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071215212253/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/multimedia/photo_gallery/0712/cfb.upsets/content.10.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=December 15, 2007}}</ref> In the game, Edwards threw for 227 yards and three touchdowns while also totaling 62 yards and a touchdown on the ground. On December 7, in a semifinal playoff game against [[Richmond Spiders football|Richmond]], Edwards set the single game FCS rushing record for a quarterback, rushing for 313 yards and 4 touchdowns on 31 carries.<ref>{{Cite web |date=December 8, 2007 |title=Edwards' dominating night puts Appalachian State in title game, 55–35 over Richmond |url=http://www.iht.com/articles/ap/2007/12/08/sports/FBC-Richmond-Appalachian-St.php |access-date=December 4, 2008 |publisher=International Herald Tribune |agency=Associated Press}}</ref> He also completed 14-of-16 passes for 192 yards and 3 touchdowns. Edwards had been mentioned as a possible candidate for the [[Heisman Trophy]] in the 2008 season.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Stewart Mandel |date=December 13, 2008 |title=Edwards for Heisman? |publisher=Sports Illustrated |url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/2007/writers/stewart_mandel/12/13/armanti.edwards/index.html |url-status=dead |access-date=December 4, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081206111104/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/2007/writers/stewart_mandel/12/13/armanti.edwards/index.html |archive-date=December 6, 2008}}</ref> Edwards established himself as a threat through the air and along the ground, and garnered elite status within the division. He and the Mountaineers won a third consecutive national championship, beating the [[University of Delaware|Delaware]] [[Delaware Fightin' Blue Hens football|Fightin' Blue Hens]], 49–21, in the [[2007 NCAA Division I Football Championship Game|championship game]] on December 14. He outplayed future [[Baltimore Ravens]] quarterback [[Joe Flacco]] in that game.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Appalachian Sports Information |date=December 14, 2007 |title=Thrice is Nice: Apps Rout Delaware For Third-Straight National Title |publisher=GoASU |url=http://www.goasu.com/ViewArticle.dbml?SPSID=104458&SPID=12811&DB_OEM_ID=21500&ATCLID=1545029 |access-date=January 4, 2008}}</ref>

[[Image:Armanti Edwards Throw.jpg|thumb|left|200px|Edwards warms up prior to a game against [[Jacksonville University]] in 2008.]]

===2008 season===
[[Image:Armanti Edwards 20081004.jpg|thumb|right|200px|Edwards (#14) with Pierre Banks (#31) in 2008.]]
The Mountaineers began the [[2008 Appalachian State Mountaineers football team|2008]] campaign against the [[LSU Tigers football|LSU Tigers]], the first time defending FBS and FCS champions have met to open the season.<ref>{{Cite news |date=August 30, 2008 |title=Edwards runs for 160 yards as Appalachian St. overwhelms No. 7 LSU |publisher=ESPN |agency=Associated Press |url=http://sports.espn.go.com/ncf/recap?gameId=282430099 |url-status=dead |access-date=September 22, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080912092818/http://sports.espn.go.com/ncf/recap?gameId=282430099 |archive-date=September 12, 2008}}</ref> However, LSU prevailed 41–13, with Edwards accounting for 216 of Appalachian State's 472 total yards. Edwards accounted for 440 yards of total offense, becoming the Southern Conference's all-time leader in yards with a 70–24 victory over the [[Wofford Terriers]] on October 31.<ref>{{Cite news ===2009 season===
Before the start of the [[2009 Appalachian State Mountaineers football team|season]], Edwards was involved in a [[Lawn mower|lawn mowing]] accident, resulting in a trip to the hospital where he was treated and released.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Tommy Bowman |date=August 7, 2009 |title=Injury to right foot sidelines Edwards |publisher=Winston-Salem Journal |url=https://www.journalnow.com/sports/college/injury-to-right-foot-sidelines-edwards/article_29899901-8c58-52a7-b8fd-5977280ba023.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191003011750/https://www.journalnow.com/sports/college/injury-to-right-foot-sidelines-edwards/article_29899901-8c58-52a7-b8fd-5977280ba023.html |archive-date=October 3, 2019}}</ref> The injury sidelined him for the season opener against the [[East Carolina Pirates football|East Carolina Pirates]], a game which the Mountaineers would lose 29–24. With a 27–10 victory over Elon on November 14, Edwards became the only quarterback in conference history to win four consecutive championships.<ref name="5Titles" /> Edwards's college football career ended on December 12 in a [[2009 NCAA Division I FCS football season#Postseason|playoff semi-final]] game against the [[Montana Grizzlies football|Montana Grizzlies]]. The 24–17 loss was the highest rated FCS postseason game ever broadcast according to [[Nielsen ratings|Nielsen]] and the NCAA.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Appalachian Sports Information |date=December 15, 2009 |title=ASU-Montana the Highest-Rated FCS Broadcast Ever |publisher=GoASU |url=http://www.goasu.com/ViewArticle.dbml?SPSID=104458&SPID=12811&DB_OEM_ID=21500&ATCLID=204858434 |access-date=April 24, 2010}}</ref> The following day, Edwards graduated after just three and a half years with a degree in [[Graphic design|graphic arts]]. On December 17, in a landslide victory, Edwards received the [[Walter Payton Award]] making him the first ever two-time recipient of the award.<ref name="AEPayton2" /> On August 24, 2023, Appalachian State announced it would be retiring Edwards No. 14 jersey number.<ref>{{Cite web |date=August 24, 2023 |title=App State to Retire Armanti Edwards' Number 14 |url=https://appstatesports.com/news/2023/8/24/football-app-state-to-retire-armanti-edwards-number-14.aspx |access-date=August 24, 2023 |website=App State Athletics |language=en}}</ref>

===Carolina Panthers===
Edwards was selected in the third round, pick #89, of the 2010 draft by the [[Carolina Panthers]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2010 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2010/draft.htm |access-date=May 13, 2023 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Sommers, Erik |date=September 19, 2017 |title=CSR exclusive interview with former Panthers receiver Armanti Edwards |agency=Cat Scratch Reader |url=https://www.catscratchreader.com/2017/9/19/16324762/interview-with-former-appalachian-state-qb-carolina-panthers-wr-wide-receiver-armanti-edwards |url-status=live |access-date=September 22, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170922145349/https://www.catscratchreader.com/2017/9/19/16324762/interview-with-former-appalachian-state-qb-carolina-panthers-wr-wide-receiver-armanti-edwards |archive-date=September 22, 2017}}</ref> It was reported that Edwards could see the field at a variety of positions including [[wide receiver]], [[kickoff returner]], and quarterback in the [[wildcat formation]]. He was first activated in the 2010 season for the October 10 game against the [[Chicago Bears]]. After a 34–3 loss against New Orleans and the loss of [[Matt Moore (American football)|Matt Moore]] to the injured reserve list, Coach [[John Fox (American football)|John Fox]] hinted that Edwards would see more snaps at quarterback in practice. Edwards was named the emergency/third quarterback for the first time before the November 14 game at [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers|Tampa Bay]], behind new starter [[Jimmy Clausen]] and backup [[Tony Pike]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.nfl.com/news/out-of-options-clausen-to-start-at-qb-for-panthers-vs-bucs-09000d5d81c024a5 | title=Out of options: Clausen to start at QB for Panthers vs. Bucs | publisher=[[NFL.com]] | date=Nov 10, 2010 | accessdate=7 May 2026}}</ref> Like Moore the week before, Clausen also suffered an injury.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.panthers.com/news/quarterback-questions-continue-3074082 | title=Quarterback questions continue | publisher=[[Carolina Panthers]] | date=Nov 22, 2010 | accessdate=7 May 2026 | author=Strickland, Bryan}}</ref> For the team's next game on November 21 against [[Baltimore Ravens|Baltimore]], Edwards was again listed as the third-string quarterback; this time behind new starter [[Brian St. Pierre]] and backup Tony Pike.<ref name="Yasinskas">{{cite web | url=https://www.espn.com/blog/nflnation/post/_/id/31894/armanti-edwards-third-qb-for-panthers | title=Armanti Edwards third QB for Panthers | publisher=[[ESPN.com]] | date=November 21, 2010 | accessdate=7 May 2026 | author=Yasinskas, Pat}}</ref> On December 12, Edwards featured at quarterback for one snap against the [[Atlanta Falcons]] completing a pass to fellow rookie [[David Gettis]] for no gain.

Edwards mostly played wide receiver, kick returner, and punt returner during his time with the Panthers. He was released on October 8, 2013.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wesseling |first=Chris |date=October 8, 2013 |title=Armanti Edwards to be released by Carolina Panthers |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/armanti-edwards-to-be-released-by-carolina-panthers-0ap2000000259331 |access-date=August 17, 2014 |website=NFL.com}}</ref>

===Toronto Argonauts===
On May 27, 2017, Edwards was traded from the Roughriders to the [[Toronto Argonauts]] in exchange for offensive lineman, [[Peter Dyakowski]].<ref name="v278">{{cite web | title=Argos acquire WR Edwards in trade with Riders | website=Toronto Argonauts | date=2017-05-28 | url=https://www.argonauts.ca/2017/05/27/argos-acquire-wr-edwards-trade-riders/ | access-date=2025-01-01}}</ref> Edwards had a breakout season in [[2017 CFL season|2017]] for the Argos, playing in all but one regular season game, catching 83 passes for 962 yards with four touchdowns. In the playoffs he caught seven passes for 56 yards en route to winning the [[105th Grey Cup]]. In January 2018 Edwards and the Argos agreed to a new two-year contract.<ref>{{Cite news |date=January 15, 2018 |title=Argos re-sign WR Edwards to 2-year deal – Article – TSN |work=TSN |url=https://www.tsn.ca/argos-re-sign-wr-edwards-to-2-year-deal-1.968458 |access-date=January 15, 2018}}</ref> Edwards finished 2018 with a similar statistical line as 2017, with 4 receiving touchdowns and coming up just shy of 1,000 yards; however, the Argos went from first to worst, following up their 2017 championship with a league worst 4–14 record for 2018. 2019 saw the Argonauts with the same record, but Edwards eclipsed the 1,000 mark for the first time, and caught seven touchdowns. He became a free agent once his contract expired on February 11, 2020.

===XFL===
Edwards signed with the [[XFL (2020)|XFL]]'s [[Team 9 (XFL)|Team 9]] [[practice squad]] on February 19, 2020.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Nagashima, Matthew |date=February 19, 2020 |title=CFL Veteran WR Armanti Edwards Signs With XFL Team Nine |work=XFLNewsHub.com |url=https://www.xflnewshub.com/xfl-news/cfl-veteran-armanti-edwards-xfl/ |access-date=February 19, 2020}}</ref> He was signed off of Team 9 by the [[Dallas Renegades]] on February 25, 2020.<ref>{{Cite tweet |number=1232353029615161345 |user=XFLRenegades |title=ROSTER UPDATE: The Renegades have made 3 roster moves this week, adding WR Armanti Edwards, OLB Jesse Aniebonam, and QB Brogan Roback. WR Jerrod Heard was waived. OLB Hau'oli Kikaha has retired. QB Eric Dungey was placed on the Reserve/Left Squad list due to a family matter. |date=February 25, 2020 |access-date=February 25, 2020}}</ref> He had his contract terminated when the league suspended operations on April 10, 2020.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Condotta, Bob |date=April 10, 2020 |title=XFL suspends operations, terminates all employees, but Jim Zorn says he has hopes league will continue |work=SeattleTimes.com |url=https://www.seattletimes.com/sports/xfl-suspends-operations-terminates-all-employees/ |access-date=July 17, 2020}}</ref>

As a former player at a high level, Carl was not supportive of the idea of his son entering the sport at such a young age. Foster took to the game, telling his elementary school teacher that he intended to become "a star in the NFL."{{Cite web |title=JockBio: Arian Foster Biography |url=http://www.jockbio.com/Bios/A_Foster/A_Foster_bio.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150720185041/http://www.jockbio.com/Bios/A_Foster/A_Foster_bio.html |archive-date=July 20, 2015 |access-date=August 8, 2015 |website=jockbio.com}} Foster attended Taft Middle School in Albuquerque.{{Cite web |date=September 26, 2010 |title=NFL Star Arian Foster Has Mixed Memories Of The Duke City, But He Wants To Help Its Kids |url=https://www.abqjournal.com/232764/nfl-star-arian-foster-has-mixed-memories-of-the-duke-city-but-he-wants-to-help-its-kids.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201008181850/https://www.abqjournal.com/232764/nfl-star-arian-foster-has-mixed-memories-of-the-duke-city-but-he-wants-to-help-its-kids.html |archive-date=October 8, 2020 |access-date=October 8, 2020 |website=Albuquerque Journal |language=en-US}} His parents divorced in 2000 while he was attending [[Valley High School (New Mexico)|Valley High School]] in Albuquerque, and in 2002, he moved to San Diego with his father. Foster competed in [[high school football|football]] at [[Mission Bay Senior High School]], where he initially played as a linebacker, but became a full-time running back in his junior and senior years.{{Cite web |last=Jenkins |first=Chris |date=2013-08-30 |title=Arian Foster: A "vision" from Mission Bay |url=https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2013/08/30/arian-foster-a-vision-from-mission-bay/ |access-date=2024-12-27 |website=San Diego Union-Tribune |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |last=Robertson |first=Dale |date=2013-09-09 |title=Foster's success grows from deep San Diego roots |url=https://www.houstonchronicle.com/sports/texans/article/foster-s-success-grows-from-deep-san-diego-roots-4797581.php |access-date=2024-12-27 |website=Houston Chronicle |language=en}} He was Mission Bay's featured running back those years, and led [[San Diego County]] in all-purpose yards with 2,500 while compiling 2,093 rushing yards and 24 touchdowns in addition to six scores on kickoff returns his senior year.{{Cite web |title=Arian Foster |url=http://www.utsports.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/foster_arian00.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=http://www.freezepage.com/1317965556DBVBAQOBBM?url=http://www.utsports.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/foster_arian00.html |archive-date=October 7, 2011 |access-date=October 7, 2011 |website=University of Tennessee Athletics}} In a game against [[Clairemont High School]], Foster ran for 321 yards and for his efforts, he was named ''[[San Diego Union Tribune]]'' All-San Diego Western League Player of the Year, received All-West Region appointment by ''[[PrepStar]]'', and also earned All-California Interscholastic Federation honors. He earned a three-star rating from [[Rivals.com]]. Then-Tennessee offensive coordinator [[Randy Sanders]] and running backs coach [[Trooper Taylor]] were impressed by Foster when recruiting in [[San Diego]].{{Cite web |last=Martin |first=Jeffrey |date=September 17, 2010 |title=Unorthodox Foster provides Texans with dynamic RB |url=https://www.chron.com/sports/texans/article/Unorthodox-Foster-provides-Texans-with-dynamic-RB-1713708.php |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160103124315/http://www.chron.com/sports/texans/article/Unorthodox-Foster-provides-Texans-with-dynamic-RB-1713708.php |archive-date=January 3, 2016 |access-date=April 19, 2020 |website=The Houston Chronicle}} Foster committed to attend Tennessee on January 28, 2004.{{Cite web |title=Arian Foster - Rivals.com |url=https://n.rivals.com/content/prospects/2004/arian-foster-29395 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170711115228/https://n.rivals.com/content/prospects/2004/arian-foster-29395 |archive-date=July 11, 2017 |access-date=February 16, 2018 |website=Rivals.com}} Foster also competed on the [[track & field]] team as a sprinter and high jumper. He had personal-bests of 11.24 seconds in the [[dash]], and had a top-jump of 6'2.5" in the [[high jump]]. He was also a member of the [[4 x 100 metres relay|4 × 100 m]] relay squad.{{Cite web |title=Arian Foster |url=https://www.trackingfootball.com/players/arian-foster-7027/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141023175134/https://www.trackingfootball.com/players/arian-foster-7027/ |archive-date=October 23, 2014 |access-date=August 8, 2015 |website=trackingfootball.com}} ==College career== Foster [[Redshirt (college sports)|red-shirted]] his first season at the [[University of Tennessee]], sitting behind [[Gerald Riggs Jr.]] and [[Cedric Houston]] on the depth chart.{{Cite news |date=December 8, 2005 |title=Foster Duo Named to SEC Coaches' All-Freshman Squad |url=https://utsports.com/news/2005/12/8/FOSTER_DUO_NAMED_TO_SEC_COACHES_ALL_FRESHMAN_SQUAD.aspx |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181105202847/https://utsports.com/news/2005/12/8/FOSTER_DUO_NAMED_TO_SEC_COACHES_ALL_FRESHMAN_SQUAD.aspx |archive-date=November 5, 2018 |access-date=November 5, 2018 |work=University of Tennessee Athletics}} He was a three-year starter at [[running back]] for the [[Tennessee Volunteers football|Volunteers]].{{Cite web |title=Arian Foster College Stats |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/arian-foster-1.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180216085130/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/arian-foster-1.html |archive-date=February 16, 2018 |access-date=February 16, 2018 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}} ===2005 season=== In his 2005 redshirt freshman season, Foster was an immediate contributor. He only had one game with 100 rushing yards, the second game of the season, a 35–3 victory over the [[2008 UAB Blazers football team|UAB Blazers]].{{Cite web |title=UAB at Tennessee Box Score, September 13, 2008 |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/boxscores/2008-09-13-tennessee.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201005203741/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/boxscores/2008-09-13-tennessee.html |archive-date=October 5, 2020 |access-date=February 16, 2018 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}} For his part, Fulmer would attribute Foster's diminished workload to knee and thigh injuries which would later be disputed. In the end, Foster compiled 570 yards on 131 carries with just one touchdown in his senior season.{{Cite web |title=Arian Foster 2008 Game Log |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/arian-foster-1/gamelog/2008/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180216085124/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/arian-foster-1/gamelog/2008/ |archive-date=February 16, 2018 |access-date=February 16, 2018 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}} Foster finished his collegiate career as the school's second all-time leading rusher with 2,964 yards, only trailing [[Travis Henry]].{{Cite web |title=Tennessee Volunteers Rushing |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/tennessee/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180318121052/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/tennessee/ |archive-date=March 18, 2018 |access-date=April 19, 2020 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}} His legacy, however, was mixed. He fumbled just five times on a school-record 650 carries, but all of them came at critical moments. His former coach Fulmer has defended Foster regarding these crucial mistakes, saying "There were a couple of fumbles that were untimely that people want to remember; they forget about his full career, about how special he was. He had a couple of fumbles after a couple of big runs. They were costly, but we probably wouldn't have been there without him." Among all players in Tennessee history to reach 1,000 rushing yards, Foster finished second in receiving yards in school history with 742, only trailing [[Stanley Morgan]]. ==Professional career== ===Pre-draft=== Foster's subpar senior campaign caused his draft stock to plummet, as well as scouts' concerns about his below-average pass-blocking, issues with ball security, and the less-than-stellar reviews from Tennessee staff members that portrayed him as selfish and hard to coach.{{Citation |title=Scout Talk: Arian Foster |date=September 19, 2010 |publisher=National Football Post}} Foster ranked 24th among running backs available in the [[2009 NFL draft]], according to ''[[Sports Illustrated]]''.{{Cite web |title=View Draft by Positions |url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/football/2009/draft/breakdowns/by_position/RB.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090420070922/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/football/2009/draft/breakdowns/by_position/RB.html |archive-date=April 20, 2009 |website=CNN.com}} A pulled hamstring prevented Foster from working out at the [[NFL Scouting Combine]], and he had a poor showing at Tennessee's Pro Day when he registered a 4.65 40-yard dash, 4.50 short shuttle, 32" vertical leap and 9′7″ broad jump. '''Arrelious Markus Benn''' (born September 8, 1988) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Illinois Fighting Illini football|Illinois Fighting Illini]] and was selected by the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] in the second round of the [[2010 NFL draft]].

==Early life==
A native of [[Washington, DC]], Benn attended [[Dunbar High School (Washington, D.C.)|Dunbar High School]] in the [[Truxton Circle]] neighborhood, where he was teammates with [[Vontae Davis]] and [[Nate Bussey]]. Benn played wide receiver, [[running back]], [[Safety (American football position)|safety]], and [[linebacker]] in high school, and was named a First-team High School [[All-America]]n his senior season.  That year, Benn caught 56 passes for 1,039 yards and nine touchdowns, the first Dunbar player to ever crack the 1,000 yard mark.  During his junior season in high school, Benn caught 50 passes for 1,147 yards and 17 touchdowns.  Following his high school career, Benn was invited to play in the 2007 [[U.S. Army All-American Bowl]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://footballrecruiting.rivals.com/content.asp?SID=880&CID=754975#2007| title=2007 U.S. Army All-American Bowl Roster| publisher=[[Rivals.com]]| access-date=January 24, 2007}}</ref>

Regarded as a five-star recruit by ''[[Rivals.com]]'', Benn was ranked as the No. 5 wide receiver prospect in the class of 2007, behind [[Ronald Johnson (American football)|Ronald Johnson]], [[Terrence Toliver]], [[Chris Culliver]], and [[Dwight Jones (American football)|Dwight Jones]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://sports.yahoo.com/ncaa/football/recruiting/rankings/rank-1517|title=Rivals.com|website=sports.yahoo.com}}</ref> Benn chose Illinois over [[Maryland Terrapins football|Maryland]], [[Notre Dame Fighting Irish football|Notre Dame]], [[Miami Hurricanes football|Miami (FL)]], and [[Florida State Seminoles football|Florida State]].

==College career==
During his freshman season at the [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign]], Benn caught 43 passes for 521 yards (54 passes for 676 yards including the Rose Bowl appearance by the [[Illinois Fighting Illini football|Fighting Illini]] that season); this was the team high for the season and a school record for a freshman. Benn also added 158 yards on 32 carries on the ground, along with returning 10 kickoffs for 280 yards, including a 90-yard kickoff return for touchdown against Penn State, one of his two touchdowns that day.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Klein |first=Gary |date=December 3, 2007 |title=USC-Illinois accents Rose Bowl tradition |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2007-dec-03-sp-rose3-story.html |access-date=March 6, 2024 |website=Los Angeles Times |language=en-US}}</ref>  He was named the 2007 [[Big Ten]] Freshman of the Year.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.illinoisloyalty.com/Forums/archive/index.php/t-4701.html|title=2007 Big Ten Awards – Mendenhall, O'Donnell, Benn, Leman, V Davis, Zook [Archive] – Fighting Illini Forums|website=www.illinoisloyalty.com|date=September 8, 2023 }}</ref>

During his sophomore campaign, Benn's stats improved to 67 rec and a Big Ten-leading 1055 yards, along with 3 touchdowns through the air, and also contributed to the run game with 101 yards on 23 carries, with 2 rushing touchdowns. On August 10, 2009, Benn was named to the Walter Camp "Players to Watch" list for its prestigious Player of the Year award, the nation's fourth-oldest individual college football accolade. On August 12, 2009, Benn was named to 2009 Biletnikoff Trophy Watch list.

As a junior, Benn suffered a right ankle sprain in the season opener against Missouri,<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.espn.com/chicago/columns/story?id=4518611&columnist=powers_scott| title=Don't forget about me| date=September 30, 2009| publisher=[[ESPN]]| access-date=September 16, 2016}}</ref> and played injured the rest of the season, appearing in all 12 games, but accumulating only 38 receptions for 490 yards and two touchdowns through the air, to go with 7 carries for 23 yards and one touchdown on the ground.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Arrelious Benn College Stats, School, Draft, Gamelog, Splits |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/arrelious-benn-1.html |access-date=March 6, 2024 |website=College Football at Sports-Reference.com |publisher=[[Sports-Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

On December 16, 2009, following his junior season, Arrelious Benn announced his decision to enter the [[2010 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Citation |first=Shannon |last=Ryan |newspaper=Chicago Tribune |date=December 17, 2009 |title=Illinois' Arrelious Benn heading to the NFL |url=http://www.chicagotribune.com/sports/college/chi-17-illinois-arrelious-benn-dec17,0,4100380.story |access-date=December 21, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091220041553/http://www.chicagotribune.com/sports/college/chi-17-illinois-arrelious-benn-dec17,0,4100380.story |archive-date=December 20, 2009 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

===Philadelphia Eagles===
On March 15, 2013, Benn was traded to the [[Philadelphia Eagles]], along with a 7th-round pick, for a 2013 6th-round pick and a 2014 conditional pick.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.philadelphiaeagles.com/news/article-1/Eagles-Acquire-WR-Arrelious-Benn/11de3f65-4a30-49f3-b0e0-5d12dc3b8a16|title=Eagles Acquire WR Arrelious Benn|access-date=March 15, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130318024456/http://www.philadelphiaeagles.com/news/article-1/Eagles-Acquire-WR-Arrelious-Benn/11de3f65-4a30-49f3-b0e0-5d12dc3b8a16|archive-date=March 18, 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref> On March 21, 2013, Benn signed a one-year contract extension through 2014. On August 6, 2013, Benn tore his ACL.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/arrelious-benn-tears-acl-philadelphia-eagles-thinner-0ap1000000227063 |title=Arrelious Benn tears ACL; Philadelphia Eagles thinner |last=Wesseling |first=Chris |date=August 6, 2013 |website=NFL.com |access-date=August 7, 2013}}</ref> On August 7, 2013, Benn was placed on the Injured Reserve list, which officially ended his 2013 season.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.philadelphiaeagles.com/news/article-1/Arrelious-Benn-Placed-On-Injured-Reserve/8651e877-5d37-404c-882a-d330e5c66bcf |title=Arrelious Benn Placed On Injured Reserve |last=McPherson |first=Chris |date=August 7, 2013 |website=PhiladelphiaEagles.com |access-date=August 8, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130810223542/http://www.philadelphiaeagles.com/news/article-1/Arrelious-Benn-Placed-On-Injured-Reserve/8651e877-5d37-404c-882a-d330e5c66bcf |archive-date=August 10, 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref> He was released by the Eagles on May 16, 2014.<ref name="l483">{{cite web | last=Patra | first=Kevin | title=Philadelphia Eagles cut wide receiver Arrelious Benn | website=NFL.com | date=2014-05-16 | url=https://www.nfl.com/news/philadelphia-eagles-cut-wide-receiver-arrelious-benn-0ap2000000350918 | access-date=2024-11-29}}</ref> Benn was re-signed by Philadelphia on May 19. Benn was placed on injured reserve on August 30, 2014. He played [[college football]] for the [[Ole Miss Rebels football|Ole Miss Rebels]].

==Early life and college career==
Born in [[Oxford, Mississippi]], Spearman grew up in [[Bruce, Mississippi]] and was an honorable mention [[USA Today All-USA high school football team|''USA Today'' All-American]] linebacker as a senior in 1995.<ref name="pfa"/><ref name="Ole Miss">{{cite web|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20000816205107/http://olemisssports.fansonly.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/spearman_armegis00.html|archivedate=August 16, 2000|title=Armegis Spearman|publisher=University of Mississippi|url=http://olemisssports.fansonly.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/spearman_armegis00.html|accessdate=October 10, 2020}}</ref>

He played college football at the [[University of Mississippi]] where he was selected named to the Freshman All-SEC team in 1996.  In both his junior and senior seasons in 1998 and 1999, he earned second-team All-SEC honors.  After graduating with a B.A. in Business Administration, Spearman was invited to play in the Hula Bowl.<ref name="Ole Miss"/> However, he fell one vote short of being invited to the NFL Scouting Combine.

==Professional career==
Spearman said that his agent was contacted by several teams during the draft and was told continually that teams were considering drafting him, including the [[Green Bay Packers]] and [[New England Patriots]] in the third round. In the end, though, Spearman went undrafted. He received interest from 21 different teams. Spearman had been so impressed by his meetings with Cincinnati Bengals linebacker coach [[Mark Duffner]] that he chose to sign with the Bengals on a two-year contract with a $10,000 signing bonus.

As soon as camp opened, Spearman impressed the Bengals coaching staff with his size, strength, and instincts. He began his rookie season playing primarily on special teams, but after an injury to starting middle linebacker [[Brian Simmons]], Spearman was inserted into the starting lineup and had an outstanding season, logging 70 tackles. He was selected to the 2000 NFL All-Rookie Team.

Coming off such a promising rookie campaign, Spearman was poised to become a centerpiece in the Bengals defense. However, he suffered a torn pectoral muscle and missed the entire 2001 season. Again, in 2002, he was bitten by the injury bug. After overcoming a hamstring injury suffered in the preseason finale, Spearman appeared in only seven games when an ankle injury landed him back on Injured Reserve on November 1, 2002.

As a restricted free agent after the 2002 season, Spearman received an offer of $550,000 from the Packers. The Bengals elected to match the offer and retain him. However, Spearman struggled with injuries throughout training camp and was released by first year head coach [[Marvin Lewis]]. Two days later, Spearman was signed by the [[Houston Texans]]. However, he was released by the Texans on September 10, 2003.

On April 14, 2004, the Packers signed Spearman. He was released the day before training camp started, and his professional career was essentially over.

==Post-football career==
In 2012, Spearman enrolled in [[Master of Education]] studies at [[Central Methodist University]], an NAIA school in [[Fayette, Missouri]], and served as a graduate assistant linebackers coach for [[Central Methodist Eagles football]]. The team promoted Spearman to full-time linebackers coach the following year.<ref name="learning specialist">{{cite web|url=https://olemisssports.com/staff-directory/armegis-spearman/208|title=Armegis Spearman: Learning Specialist|publisher=University of Mississippi|accessdate=October 10, 2020}}</ref>

Spearman transferred to the University of Mississippi in 2014 to pursue an M.A. in higher education with a concentration in student personnel and work as a mentor in the Student-Athlete Success Center.<ref name="learning specialist"/> Spearman became a learning specialist in 2016 and completed his M.A. in 2018.<ref name="learning specialist"/>

'''Armon Tyrae Binns''' (born September 8, 1989) is an American [[American football|football]] coach and former [[wide receiver]]. He is currently the wide receivers coach for the [[Northwestern Wildcats football|Northwestern Wildcats]]. He played [[college football]] at [[Cincinnati Bearcats football|Cincinnati]]. Binns was signed by the [[Jacksonville Jaguars]] as an undrafted free agent in 2011. He has also been a member of the [[Cincinnati Bengals]], [[Miami Dolphins]], [[Kansas City Chiefs]], and [[Ottawa Redblacks]].

==Early life==
Binns graduated from [[Pasadena High School (California)|Pasadena High School]] in 2007, where he starred in football and basketball.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2007-feb-13-sp-sondcol13-story.html|title=Pasadena's Binns didn't go the Cliffs Notes route|website=[[Los Angeles Times]]|date=13 February 2007}}</ref> Binns and his wife, Lauren, who has a bachelor's degree from UC Berkeley, have three children—Noah, Eli, and Eden.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://gobearcats.com/sports/football/roster/staff/armon-binns/78|title=Armon Binns - Quality Control - Offense - Football Support Staff}}</ref> They started dating when Armon was a junior at the University of Cincinnati; they were married in 2011.

==College career==
As a wide receiver for the Cincinnati Bearcats, Binns finished the [[2009 Cincinnati Bearcats football team|2009 season]] with 61 receptions for 888 yards and 11 touchdowns.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/player/_/id/14223/armon-binns|title=Armon Binns Stats, News, Bio}}</ref> He was on the watch list for the [[Biletnikoff Award]] during the 2009 season. He scored a touchdown on a 29-yard pass from [[Tony Pike]] for the go-ahead score with 33 seconds left in the 2009 River City Rivalry against the [[University of Pittsburgh]], which the Bearcats won 45-44.

Binns started all 12 games as a senior and posted a team-high 75 receptions for 1,101 yards with 10 touchdowns. He also led the [[Big East Conference (1979–2013)|Big East]] in receptions, receiving yards, receptions per game (6.2) and receiving yards per game (91.8).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/player/stats/_/id/14223/armon-binns|title=Armon Binns Stats}}</ref>

==Professional career==
===Cincinnati Bengals===
Binns was signed to the [[Cincinnati Bengals]]' [[practice squad]] on September 20, 2011. He saw game action in the 2012 season, playing in seven games (five as a starter) with 18 receptions for 210 receiving yards and one touchdown.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BinnAr00.htm|title = Armon Binns Stats|website = [[Pro-Football-Reference.com]]}}</ref>

===Miami Dolphins===
Binns was claimed off waivers by the [[Miami Dolphins]] on December 10, 2012.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.foxnews.com/sports/dolphins-claim-wr-binns-from-bengals/|title=Dolphins claim WR Binns from Bengals|website=[[Fox News]]|date=27 March 2015}}</ref> Playing for the Dolphins the remainder of the season, Binns caught six passes for 67 yards.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BinnAr00.htm|title = Armon Binns Stats|website = [[Pro-Football-Reference.com]]}}</ref>

On July 28, 2013, Binns suffered a torn ACL and MCL during the Dolphins' training camp, forcing him to miss the entire 2013 season.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.palmbeachpost.com/news/sports/football/miami-dolphins-coach-joe-philbin-says-rookie-dion-/nY6Xp/|work=Palm Beach Post|title=Miami Dolphins coach Philbin says Rooki Dion|access-date=2013-07-29|archive-date=2013-08-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130802163450/http://www.palmbeachpost.com/news/sports/football/miami-dolphins-coach-joe-philbin-says-rookie-dion-/nY6Xp/|url-status=dead}}</ref> On July 31, 2013, Binns was waived/injured by the Miami Dolphins.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.miamidolphins.com/news/press-releases/article-1/PRESS-RELEASE-Dolphins-Make-Roster-Moves/5d46c1ce-7862-43bb-99fe-9e97ad9b03da |title=PRESS RELEASE: Dolphins Make Roster Moves |date=July 31, 2013 |website=MiamiDolphins.com |access-date=July 31, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130801190421/http://www.miamidolphins.com/news/press-releases/article-1/PRESS-RELEASE-Dolphins-Make-Roster-Moves/5d46c1ce-7862-43bb-99fe-9e97ad9b03da |archive-date=August 1, 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Binns was placed on Injured/Reserve on August 1, 2013. The Dolphins released Binns on August 26, 2014.<ref>{{cite tweet|number=504363291884666880|user=MiamiDolphins|title=The team has announced the following roster moves:<!-- full text of tweet that Twitter returned to the bot (excluding links) added by TweetCiteBot. This may be better truncated or may need expanding (TW limits responses to 140 characters) or case changes. --> |date=26 August 2014}}</ref>

===Kansas City Chiefs===
The [[Kansas City Chiefs]] signed Binns to their [[practice squad]] on September 8, 2014.<ref>[http://www.kansascity.com/sports/nfl/kansas-city-chiefs/article1907731.html Chiefs sign receiver Armon Binns to the practice squad]</ref> On December 31, 2014, Binns signed a [[futures contract]] with the Chiefs.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.kcchiefs.com/news/article-2/Chiefs-Sign-19-To-ReserveFutures-Contracts/3270d295-cf1e-4ac8-8eb1-6913d08d481a |title=Chiefs Sign 19 To Reserve/Futures Contracts |access-date=February 18, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151119090658/http://www.kcchiefs.com/news/article-2/Chiefs-Sign-19-To-ReserveFutures-Contracts/3270d295-cf1e-4ac8-8eb1-6913d08d481a |archive-date=November 19, 2015 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

=== Ottawa Redblacks ===
On February 3, 2016, Binns signed a contract with the [[Ottawa Redblacks]] of the [[Canadian Football League]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Redblacks sign three players from U.S. to contracts |url=https://ottawacitizen.com/sports/football/cfl/redblacks-sign-three-players-from-u-s-to-contracts |website=Ottawa Citizen |access-date=February 6, 2016 |language=en-US |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160206005739/http://ottawacitizen.com/sports/football/cfl/redblacks-sign-three-players-from-u-s-to-contracts |archive-date=February 6, 2016 }}</ref>

==Coaching career==
For the 2018 season, Binns joined the staff of his college head coach [[Brian Kelly (American football coach)|Brian Kelly]] at [[Notre Dame Fighting Irish football|Notre Dame]] as an offensive analyst. Binns would help mentor [[Miles Boykin]] during his time in [[South Bend]].

In 2019 Binns joined [[Hampton Pirates football|Hampton]] as their [[wide receivers coach]],<ref>{{cite web |url=https://hamptonpirates.com/staff-directory/armon-binns/294 |title=Armon Binns - Wide Receivers Coach - Staff Directory - Hampton University Athletics |website=hamptonpirates.com |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200302143805/https://hamptonpirates.com/staff-directory/armon-binns/294 |archive-date=2020-03-02}}</ref> before returning to his alma mater the [[University of Cincinnati]] as a [[quality control coach]] for the 2020 season.

After two seasons at Cincinnati, Binns was hired as the receivers coach at [[Youngstown State Penguins football|Youngstown State]] in March 2022. During his time at Youngstown, Binns coached star wide receiver [[Bryce Oliver]] and helped him to become a first team all conference player. After helping lead a remarkable comeback season for the Penguins in 2022, Binns was hired as the wide receivers coach at Northwestern by [[Pat Fitzgerald]]. <ref>{{cite news |last1=Samuels |first1=Doug |title=The Scoop - Wednesday March 16, 2022 |url=https://footballscoop.com/thescoop/the-scoop-wednesday-march-16-2022 |access-date=16 March 2022 |work=footballscoop.com |publisher=Football Scoop |date=16 March 2022}}</ref>

'''Arryn Siposs''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|s|ɪ|p|ɔː|s}} {{Respell|SIP|awss}};<ref>[https://media.eagles.1rmg.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/14141740/Siposs-Arryn-2021-6.pdf Arryn Siposs (profile) – Philadelphia Eagles.] Retrieved 11 December 2022.</ref> born 25 November 1992) is an Australian former professional [[American football]] [[Punter (football)|punter]]. He is a former professional [[Australian rules football]]er who played for the [[St Kilda Football Club]] in the [[Australian Football League]] (AFL). He later [[List of players who have converted from one football code to another|switched codes]] to play [[college football]] for [[Auburn Tigers football|Auburn]].

==AFL career==
Siposs was drafted by St Kilda with the 75th selection in the [[2010 AFL draft]] from the [[Dandenong Stingrays]] in the [[Talent League|TAC Cup]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Murnane |first=Matt |date=5 May 2011 |title=Siposs the latest new boy in Saints' roll-out |url=https://www.smh.com.au/sport/afl/siposs-the-latest-new-boy-in-saints-rollout-20110505-1eab5.html |access-date=22 February 2023 |website=The Sydney Morning Herald |language=en}}</ref> He was originally from Beaconsfield and played in the South East Juniors where he kicked 99 goals in his under 16s year. Playing in the TAC Cup for the Stingrays he kicked 34 goals in 2010.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Holmesby |first=Luke |date=14 November 2012 |title=Draft memories: Arryn Siposs |url=http://www.saints.com.au/news/2012-11-15/draft-memories-arryn-siposs |access-date=20 January 2019 |website=Saints.com.au}}</ref>

Siposs made his debut against {{AFL Car}} in round 7 of the [[2011 AFL season]]. He was substituted on in the second half of the match and had four disposals and kicked one goal. The Saints lost by three points (81–84). He then played the next five games (and kicked five goals) but was dropped after the Saints lost to {{AFL Col}} by 57 points. He was then named in the squad to play against {{AFL PA}} in round 16 but was later made an emergency. Toward the end of the season, he suffered [[shin splints]].

He was delisted at the conclusion of the 2015 season.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Holmesby |first=Luke |date=22 September 2015 |title=Saints make four list changes |url=http://www.saints.com.au/news/2015-09-22/saints-make-four-list-changes |access-date=22 September 2015 |website=Saints.com.au |publisher=[[Bigpond]]}}</ref>

Chark's punt return, Auburn's Arryn Siposs understands his importance vs. LSU |url=https://www.al.com/auburnfootball/index.ssf/2018/09/arryn_siposs_settling_at_punte.html |access-date=18 October 2018 |website=AL.com}}</ref> Siposs competed for the starting punter position behind Aiden Marshall, prior to the start of the 2018 season,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Crepea |first=James |date=29 July 2018 |title=Auburn fall camp position breakdown: Specialists |url=https://www.al.com/auburnfootball/index.ssf/2018/07/auburn_fall_camp_position_brea_7.html |access-date=18 October 2018 |website=AL.com}}</ref> and was later named as backup to Marshall.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Crepea |first=James |date=28 August 2018 |title=Aidan Marshall remains Auburn's starting punter |url=https://www.al.com/auburnfootball/index.ssf/2018/08/aidan_marshall_remains_auburns.html |access-date=18 October 2018 |website=AL.com}}</ref> However, Siposs was on the field more than Marshall against the [[2018 Washington Huskies football team|Washington Huskies]], and head coach [[Gus Malzahn]] opted to make Siposs the starting punter against the [[2018 Alabama State Hornets football team|Alabama State Hornets]].<ref name="al.com" />
